# Approximations schemes for Edit Distance and LCS in quasi-strongly subquadratic time

**Abstract**

We present novel randomized approximation schemes for the Edit Distance (ED) problem and the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem that, for any constant \(\varepsilon>0\), compute a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for ED and a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for LCS in time \(n^2/2log^{\Omega(1)}(n)\) for two strings of total length at most _n_. This running time improves upon the classical quadratic-time dynamic programming algorithms by a quasi-polynomial factor.

Our results yield significant insights into fine-grained complexity: Firstly, for ED, prior work indicates that any exact algorithm cannot be improved beyond a few logarithmic factors without refuting established complexity assumptions [Abboud, Hansen, Vassilevska Williams, Williams, 2016]; our quasi-polynomial speed-up shows a separation the complexity of approximate ED from that of exact ED, even for approximation factor arbitrarily close to 1. Secondly, for LCS, obtaining similar approximation-time tradeoffs via deterministic algorithms would imply breakthrough circuit lower bounds [Chen, Goldwasser, Lyu, Rothblum, Rubinstein, 2019]; our randomized algorithm demonstrates derandomization hardness for LCS approximation.

## 1 Introduction

The _edit distance (ED)_ between two strings _X_ and _Y_ , henceforth denoted ED(_X,Y_), is the minimum number of character insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to transform _X_ to _Y_ . The complexity of edit distance and its maximization counterpart<sup>1</sup>, _longest common subsequence (LCS)_, is a long-standing, central problem in algorithm design, with important applications, especially in bioinformatics. The simple quadratic-time dynamic programming solution is core material for undergraduate algorithms; this running time has been improved by one or two log factors (depending on the exact access model) \[MP80, Gra16\]. Despite extensive research for over half a century<sup>2</sup>, no better algorithms for exact ED or LCS are known.

Indeed, in one of the flagship successes of fine-grained complexity, \[BI18\] showed that there are no exact algorithms for Edit Distance running in "truly subquadratic" time, namely it is impossible to improve by \(n^\delta\) for any constant \(\delta>0\), assuming fine-grained complexity hypothesis SETH (see also e.g., \[AWW14, ABW15, BK15\]). Furthermore \[AHWW16, AB18\] showed that improving even by a few log factors would refute other fine-grained complexity assumptions and imply new circuit complexity lower bounds.

Given the limitations of exact algorithms, and especially in light of fine-grained hardness results, approximation algorithms for Edit Distance have been extensively studied: A sequence of earlier works gave super-constant-factor approximation factors in _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time \[ADG<sup>+</sup>03, BEK<sup>+</sup>03, BJKK04, BES06, OR07, AK10, AN10, AKO10, AO12\]. More recently, constant-factor approximation algorithms times were obtained by \[CDG<sup>+</sup>20, BEG<sup>+</sup>21, And20, BR20, GRS20, KS20b, AN20\]. The current state of the art has several algorithms with different trade-offs between running time and approximation (see  1). While we cannot cover all the techniques used in previous work on approximate edit distance, at a high level we seem to have hit a fundamental obstacle: all known constant-factor approximation algorithms for ED rely on a triangle inequality technique that inherently incurs at least a 3-factor in the approximation \[Rub18\]. No better-than-3-approximation algorithms are known with any non-trivial running time.

Remarkably, good multiplicative approximations for LCS are even more scarce than ED: despite significant attention (e.g., \[HSSS19, RS20, AV21, RSSS25, BCD23, HL23\]), for worst-case instances the best previous known approximation factor is just barely sub-polynomial \[Nos21\]. Furthermore, \[CGL<sup>+</sup>19\] shows that obtaining such approximation-time tradeoffs for approximate LCS with _deterministic_ algorithms would imply new breakthrough circuit lower bounds<sup>3</sup>.

### Main result

We give approximation schemes for ED and LCS, i.e., for any constant \(\varepsilon>0\), we get a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for ED and a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for LCS. Our approximation schemes run in time

\(\frac{n^2}{2^{log^{\Omega(1)}(n)}},\)

for two strings with total length _n_. This running time represents a quasi-polynomial improvement over the classical quadratic-time algorithms.

### Why this is interesting

<sup>1</sup>Technically, LCS is the complement of a variant of ED where substitutions are not allowed (or rather counted as 1 deletion + 1 insertion). <sup>2</sup>Beating the quadratic time was proposed as an open problem as early as \[CKK72\]. <sup>3</sup>Specifically, Item 3 of Theorem 1.9 of \[CGL<sup>+</sup>19\] says that if a deterministic algorithm for LCS can obtain even a much weaker _O_(polylog(_N_))-approximation guarantee in \(N^2/2^{\omega(loglogN)^3}\) time, then NTIME\[2<sup>_O(n_)</sup>\] is not contained in non-uniform NC<sup>1</sup>.

• **Algorithmic improvement:** The most obvious achievement of our main result is a quasi-polynomial improvement in running time. While the quantitative improvement is modest, in the field of fine- grained complexity quasi-polynomial [Wil18, LW17, AFK<sup>+</sup>24] and even smaller improvements (e.g., [GMW19, JX24, DMM<sup>+</sup>25]) are often celebrated as significant steps towards pinpointing the complexity of fundamental problems (and approximate ED and LCS are certainly fundamental!). More importantly, perhaps, this improvement shows the algorithmic potential of our new structural insights (see discussion below on "tree total deviation").<tbc>

• **Separation between** \((1+\varepsilon)\)**-Approximate and Exact Computation (both ED and LCS):** For exact ED and LCS, prior work [AHWW16, AB18] shows that even shaving off a few logarithmic factors is highly unlikely without refuting established fine-grained complexity assumptions. Although a sequence of approximation algorithms faster than this lower bound have recently been known [CDG<sup>+</sup>20, BEG<sup>+</sup>21, And20, BR20, GRS20, KS20b, AN20], none of them achieve an approximation factor better than 3. Therefore, subject to certain circuit complexity hardness assumptions (see [AHWW16, AB18] for details), our result is the first to separate the complexity of \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation from exact computation of ED and LCS.<tbc>

• **Separation Between Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms (LCS):** For LCS, obtaining similar approximation-time tradeoffs using _deterministic_ algorithms would imply breakthrough circuit lower bounds [CGL<sup>+</sup>19] (see also [AB17, AR18]). Indeed, many randomized approximation algorithms for both LCS and ED have been proposed, but it was not clear whether this randomization was necessary. Our algorithm is the first to break the frontier of deterministic lower bounds by using randomization, thereby demonstrating a fundamental separation: subject to certain circuit complexity hardness assumptions (see [CGL<sup>+</sup>19]), randomized algorithms for approximate LCS are strictly faster than their deterministic counterparts.

## Additional related Work

In addition to aforementioned works on approximate ED and LCS on worst case inputs, many works also give improved guarantees under assumptions on the inputs such as small edit distance<sup>4</sup> [CGK16, GKS19, KS20a, BCR20, BCFN22a, BCFN22c, GKKS22, KS23, RSSS25], semi-random strings [AK12, Kus19, BSS20], or edit distance to error correcting codewords [HRS19]. See also e.g., [KR09, CGKK18, HSS19, BGS21, KPS21, CFH<sup>+</sup>21, JNW21, BCFN22b, KS24, BCFK24] for additional related works in other models.

Ideas related to the breakthrough constant factor approximation algorithm for edit distance have also been applied to related problems, such as tree edit distance [SS22] and, more recently, Frechet distance [CHZ25]. For tree edit distance, we leave it for future work whether our techniques can also apply to improve [BGHS19]’s state of the art (nearly) quadratic running time for \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation. For the Frechet distance, existing hardness of approximation results rule out polynomial savings assuming SETH [Bri14], and it remains open whether quasi-polynomial saving is possible.

Our work gives a quasi-polynomial improvement in running times for central problems of interest in fine-grained complexity. Other notable examples of fine-grained complexity with quasi-polynomial improvements include All-Pairs Shortest Paths [Wil18] (equivalent to the Min-plus matrix multiplication), online matrix-vector multiplication [LW17], and combinatorial boolean matrix multiplication [AFK<sup>+</sup>24].

<sup>4</sup>The careful reader may notice that some of these citations do not explicitly mention "small edit distance" in the title, but they give fast algorithms for solving a "gap edit distance" problem of distinguishing e.g. edit distance _k_ vs _k_<sup>1.5</sup>; this kind of gap problem is only non-trivial when \(k\checkmark n\).

## 2 High-level Technical Overview

First, note that if the actual ED or LCS is very small, say \(\varepsilon n\) for some \(\varepsilon=2^{-log^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\), there are exact algorithms with running time \(O(\varepsilon n^2)\) for both problems. Since our goal is to obtain algorithms with a running time of \(n^2/2^{log^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\), we henceforth focus on the case where the ED or LCS is at least \(\varepsilon n\) for \(\varepsilon=2^{-log^{O(1)}(n)}\).

Before we describe our main techniques for ED and LCS, we begin with a simple observation about sums of sequences and their sub-sequences (Section 2.1). This observation plays a crucial role in our algorithm, and analogous results have been applied to other areas of research, (see, for example, \[Dru13\]<sup>5</sup>, \[Pen25\]). We then setup the notation with a standard reduction to optimal path problems on a 2D grid (Section 2.2). In Section 2.3 we explain the core algorithmic idea, which suffices to get an additive approximation scheme (i.e., approximate ED or LCS to within \(\pm o(n)\)). Finally in Section 2.4 we extend those ideas to obtain multiplicative approximation schemes.

### 2.1 An Observation on Tree Total Deviation

One of our core ideas is a simple but powerful observation about sums of sequences and their sub-sequences. Suppose that we have a length-_n_ binary sequence _A_=(_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,...,a<sub>n</sub>_) for some _n_ that is the power of some number _M_. We define the (_M_-way) _tree total deviation_ as a measure of the total "unevenness" of _A_ across scales corresponding to blocks of size _M,M_<sup>2</sup>_,...,M_log_<sub>M</sub>n_.

In more detail, to define the tree total deviation, let _S_:=log_<sub>M</sub>n_ be the number of scales. For each scale \(s\in[S]\), we go through all _n/M_<sup>_S-s_+1</sup> intervals (_l,r_\] of form \(\big(M^{S-s+1}\cdot k,M^{S-s+1}\cdot(k+1)\big]\). Fixing some interval (_l,r_\], for each \(0\le i\le M-1\), let \(\sigma_i=\sum_{l+iM^{S-s}<x\le l+(i+1)M^{S-s}}a_x\). Namely, if we partition _a_<sub>(_l,r_\]</sub> into _M_ equal parts, then \(\sigma_i\) is the total sum of the _i_-th part. Let \(\sigma=\sum_{l<x\le r}a_x\). The contribution from interval (_l,r_\] to the tree total deviation is equal to

\(\sum_i|\sigma_i-\sigma/M|,\)

which is a measurement of how "uneven" the sequence \(\{\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{M-1}\}\) is.

Since _A_ is binary, it is easy to see that the local unevenness at an interval (_l,r_\] is _O(r-l_). Thus the total unevenness on a particular scale is _O(n_). Thus clearly the overall total unevenness (i.e., tree total deviation) is upper bounded by _O(n_log_<sub>M</sub>n_).

We observe, however, that for a sequence to be maximally uneven on a particular scale _s_, the density of 1’s has to be maximally different (i.e., close to either 0 or 1) at each block of width _M_<sup>_s_-1</sup>, and, intuitively, such density requirement makes it more difficult for the sequence to be maximally uneven on the remaining smaller scales. For the simplest example, suppose _n_=4 and _M_=2. We have two scales corresponding to blocks of size 2 and 4. The largest total deviation on the larger scale is achieved by _A_={0,0,1,1} or _A_={1,1,0,0}, but for both sequences the total deviations on the smaller scale become zero. We prove that this is not a coincidence:

(Ideal and informal version of Lemma 4.1) For all sequences with each entry being _O_(1) in absolute value, the overall total unevenness is roughly bounded by \(n\sqrt{\mathrm{log}_Mn}\), i.e., roughly \(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}_Mn}\) smaller than the naïve _O(n_log_<sub>M</sub>n_) upper bound. Moreover, if the total sum of the sequence is \(\varepsilon n\) and \(\varepsilon\) is at least 2<sup>-polylog(_n_)</sup>, then the total unevenness is roughly bounded by \(\varepsilon n\sqrt{\mathrm{log}_Mn}\).

## Proof Sketch

We now give a sketch of the proof for _M_=2, which contains all the techniques we need for proving the more general case but is much less tedious. The key idea is to decompose the total tree deviation into the contribution of each element, and then bound the contribution from an average element using a probabilistic argument.

Towards the goal of decomposing the total tree deviation to individual elements’ contributions, we first transform the sequence into another sequence with the same total tree deviation. Suppose we have a sequence _A_ with each entry being _O_(1) with total sum \(\varepsilon n\). Let _S_:=log<sub>2</sub>_n_ be the number of scales. For each scale \(s\in[S]\), we go through all _n/_2<sup>_S-s_+1</sup> intervals (_l,r_\] of form \(\left(2^{S-s+1}\cdot k,2^{S-s+1}\cdot(k+1)\right]\). Fix a scale _s_. For every interval (_l,r_\] on scale _s_, we divide it into two halves (_l,(l+r)/_2\] and ((_l+r)/_2_,r_\]. We let \(\sigma_L:=\sum_{l<x\le(l+r)/2}a_x\) be the sum on the left half, and \(\sigma_R:=\sum_{(l+r)/2<x\le r}a_x\) be the sum on the right half. In the case where _M_=2, we can see that the contribution from the interval to the tree total deviation is

\(|\sigma_L-(\sigma_L+\sigma_R)/2|+|\sigma_R-(\sigma_L+\sigma_R)/2|=|\sigma_L-\sigma_R|.\)

In other words, the local unevenness is simply the difference between the sums of the two halves. Notice that if we swap the two halves to obtain a new sequence, the total tree deviation does not change:

(_l,r_\] is the only interval where sums of the two halves are swapped (which does not change their difference) -- for other intervals, the sums of the two halves remain identical.

We can apply this swap to every applicable interval. Therefore, without loss of generality, we can assume that \(\sigma_L<\sigma_R\), and the contribution from the interval to the tree total deviation is

\(\sigma_R-\sigma_L=\left(\sum_{l<x\le(l+r)/2}-a_x\right)+\left(\sum_{(l+r)/2<x\le r}+a_x\right).\)

Thus, for every \(x\in(l,r]\), it contributes -_a<sub>x</sub>_ if _x_ is in the first half, and +_a<sub>x</sub>_ if _x_ is in the second half. Since (_l,r_\] is a scale-_s_ interval, the sign of _x_’s contribution depends only on the _s_-bit binary representation of (_x_-1): on scale-_s_, _x_ contributes -_a<sub>x</sub>_ if (_x_-1)’s _s_-th bit is 0, and +_a<sub>x</sub>_ if (_x_-1)’s _s_-th bit is 1. Summing up the total contribution from each index _x_ for each scale _s_, we have

\(\text{tree total deviation}=\sum_{1\le x\le n}a_x\left(\text{number of 1’s in}(x-1)\text{in binary) - (number of 0’s in}(x-1)\text{in binary)).\)

From well-known concentration bounds, for all but a small "tail" fraction of \(x\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), the numbers of 0’s and 1’s in (_x_-1) in binary do not differ by too much more than \(\sqrt{log_2n}\). Therefore, if the total sum of the sequence is \(\varepsilon n\) and \(\varepsilon\) is not too small for the tail to become significant, the total unevenness is roughly bounded by \(\varepsilon n\sqrt{log_2n}\).

## 2.2 Setup and Notation (a Fairly Standard Reduction to Shortest/Longest Path on a 2D Grid)

We reduce ED to a somewhat more general problem of finding the shortest path on a 2D grid<sup>6</sup> with diagonal short-cuts (Definition 5.1 or Fig. 1), where the weight of going from \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle u,v+1\rangle\rangle\) or \(\langle\langle u+1,v\rangle\rangle\) is always 1 (corresponding to insertion or deletion), and the weight of a _short-cut edge_ from \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle u+1,v+1\rangle\rangle\) is either 0 (corresponding to a match) or 1 (corresponding to a substitution). The goal is to find the length (sum of weights) of the shortest path from \(\langle\langle 0,0\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle n,n\rangle\rangle\). This shortest path problem corresponds to the standard DP algorithm for ED.

Similarly, we reduce LCS to a somewhat more general problem of finding the longest path on a 2D grid with diagonal short-cuts (Definition 5.2), where the weight of going from \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle u,v+1\rangle\rangle\) or \(\langle\langle u+1,v\rangle\rangle\) is always 0, and the weight of a _short-cut edge_ from \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle u+1,v+1\rangle\rangle\) is either 0 (no match) or 1 (match). The goal is to find the length of the longest path from \(\langle\langle 0,0\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle n,n\rangle\rangle\). This longest path problem corresponds to the standard DP algorithm for LCS.

We now use a 45\(^\circ\)-rotated 2<sup>-polylog_n_</sup>"system (see Fig. 2) to describe 2D grids with the transformation \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\rightarrow\langle u+v,v-u+n\rangle\) (Definition 5.3). We use \(\langle x,y\rangle\) when referring to the rotated coordinated system and refer to the x- and y-coordinates defined with respect to the first and second entries of \(\langle x,y\rangle\). In this notation, we are looking for the shortest/longest path from \(\langle 0,n\rangle\) to \(\langle 2n,n\rangle\). We use _column_ to refer to a subset \(\langle x,\cdot\rangle\) of the vertices, and _row_ for \(\langle\cdot,y\rangle\). It is easy to see that any \(\langle 0,n\rangle\)-to-\(\langle 2n,n\rangle\) path visits exactly one vertex of each column. A path _p_ in this notation can be given as a function \(p:\{0,\dots.2n\}\rightarrow\{0,\dots.2n\}\) mapping each x-coordinate to the corresponding y-coordinate. Importantly, such a rotation transform ensures that adjacent vertices the path visits differ in their rows by at most 1 (i.e., \(|p(i)-p(i-1)|\le 1\)), which will be crucial to bounding the curvature of a path.

## 2.3 The Main Idea: Sample and Round

To begin the discussion of our approaches, notice that it is possible to compute the shortest/longest path on the grid graphs exactly in a divide-and-conquer fashion: Suppose for the sub-problem on (_l,r_\], we want to know the boundary-to-boundary length of the shortest/longest path between \(\langle l,y_l\rangle\) and \(\langle r,y_r\rangle\) for every pair of rows (_y<sub>l</sub>,y<sub>r</sub>_). For a branching factor _M_, we divide the sub-problem into _M_ equal parts (_m<sub>i</sub>,m_<sub>_i_+1</sub>\] for \(m_i=l+i\cdot\frac{r-l}{M}\) and solve them recursively<sup>7</sup>. To find the optimal sub-path from \(\langle l,y_l\rangle\) and \(\langle r,y_r\rangle\), we look for the best _anchors_ (_p(m_<sub>1</sub>)_,p(m_<sub>2</sub>)_,...,p(m_<sub>_M_-1</sub>)) where _p(m<sub>i</sub>_) is the row the path visits in column _m<sub>i</sub>_ (i.e., the unique cell \(\langle m_i,p(m_i)\rangle\) that the sub-path visits). More formally, to compute the length of the shortest path<sup>8</sup> between \(\langle l,y_l\rangle\) and \(\langle r,y_r\rangle\), denoted by ans\[_l,y<sub>l</sub>,r,y<sub>r</sub>_\], we can use the following recursion:

\(\mathrm{ans}[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=\mathrm{min}_\widehat{Y}\sum_{i=1}^M\mathrm{ans}[m_{i-1},\widehat{y}_{i-1},m_i,\widehat{y}_i],\) (1)

where the minimization is over every anchor path defined by some sequence <o>_Y_</o>=(<o>_y_</o><sub>i</sub>) that satisfies

• <o>_y_</o><sub>0</sub>=_y<sub>l</sub>_ and <o>_y_</o><sub>M</sub>=_y<sub>r</sub>_;<tbc>

• For \(1\le i\le M\), \(\left|\overline{y_i}-\overline{y_{i-1}}\right|\le\frac{r-l}{M}\) .

At a high level, the algorithm for constant additive error is very simple: we sub-sample the columns<sup>9</sup> of the (rotated) grid, discarding all but a \(2^{-\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\)-fraction (this is where we get our running time saving). Specifically, starting from (0,2_n_\], we recursively partition the x-axis into equal-width intervals, with a branching factor _M_:=polylog(_n_). Ideally, this gives rise to _S_:=log_<sub>M</sub>_(2_n_) _scales_ in the divide-and- conquer recursion tree. Each scale \(s\in[S]\) contains all intervals of width 2_n/M_<sup>_S-s_</sup> on the same level<tbc>

Given a fixed good path, it is not hard to show that we can, with high probability, accurately estimate its true length by simply dividing its length in the surviving columns by the probability of survival, or more formally, we can change (1) to the following:

\(\mathrm{ans}[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=2\mathrm{min}_\widehat{Y}\sum_{i=1}^M\eta_i\mathrm{ans}[m_{i-1},\widehat{y}_{i-1},m_i,\widehat{y}_i],\) (2)

where each \(\eta_i\in\{0,1\}\) is uniformly sampled, and the _i_-th sub-interval is discarded if and only if \(\eta_i=0\).

However, the algorithm may hallucinate other paths that overfit the samples, as illustrated in Fig. 4. To handle this, we first observe that if there were only one candidate path, we would have obtained a good estimate. In general the algorithm should consider exponentially many candidate paths. But our divide-and- conquer algorithm considers the path one scale at a time, and we show that, at the granularity of a typical scale, it indeed suffices to consider just a single candidate path without losing too much precision.

The key observation driving our algorithm is that we can also restrict our attention to paths of bounded "curvature." Specifically, consider an interval (_l,r_\] with sub-intervals (_m<sub>i</sub>,m_<sub>_i_+1</sub>\] for \(m_i=l+i\cdot\frac{r-l}{M}\) . To reduce the possibility of hallucinating a path that overfits the samples, we reduce the number of candidate sequences of anchors (_p(m_<sub>1</sub>)_,p(m_<sub>2</sub>)_,...,p(m_<sub>_M_-1</sub>)) that the path _p_ can have to just one single "straight- line" sequence, ideally one where for every _i_ we have<sup>10</sup> \(p(m_i)=\left\lfloor p(l)+i\frac{p(r)-p(l)}{M}\right\rfloor\), or more formally, we modify (2) to the following:

\(\mathrm{ans}[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=2\sum_{i=1}^M\eta_i\mathrm{ans}\left[m_{i-1},\left\lfloor p(l)+(i-1)\frac{p(r)-p(l)}{M}\right\rfloor,m_i,\left\lfloor p(l)+i\frac{p(r)-p(l)}{M}\right\rfloor\right].\)

Here also the differences between ED and LCS become more important. ### Challenge 1 (LCS): vertical difference could be much larger than weight of the path For ED, we use the fact that the vertical difference |_p(l_)-_p(r_)| is at most the length of the \(\langle l,p(l)\rangle-\langle r,p(r)\rangle\) path to get a bound on the curvature of _p_ inside the interval (_l,r_]. For LCS, the vertical difference is no longer bounded by the weight of the path so locally the curvature could generally be much higher than the contribution to LCS. Intuitively, we can simply discard intervals with very high curvature compared to low contribution to the LCS. To bound the total error incurred by discarding such intervals, we introduce a scaled variant of the tree total deviation (Section 4.2). We use it to show that indeed most of the contribution to LCS comes from segments of the path where the ratio between curvature and weight is bounded, so we can safely discard the remaining segments. ### Challenge 2 (ED+LCS): uneven contribution from sub-paths For a fixed candidate path, if we simply split it into _M_ parts with equal widths, sample a random subset of _M/_2 parts, and let our estimate be twice the answer in the sample, one would hope that the estimate would concentrate around the true sum. However, this concentration may not hold when the sub-paths on different parts have very different weights; e.g., in the extreme case, the sub-path in one of the _M_ parts has a much higher weight than the rest combined, and the estimate would fluctuate greatly based on whether this part is in the sample or not. Fortunately, if we apply the total tree deviation result on the "weight distribution" of the path, we can also see that on average, the sub-paths should not differ too much in lengths. It turns out that it suffices to obtain an estimate that satisfies the following desiderata: • The estimate is "(nearly) sound", i.e., it does not underestimate the answer for ED (by less than (1-_o_(1))), and does not overtimate the answer for LCS (by more than (1+_o_(1))). • As long as the sub-paths do not differ too much in lengths, the estimate is also "(nearly) complete" , i.e., it does not overestimate the answer for ED (by more than (1+_o_(1))), and does not underestimate the answer for LCS (by less than (1-_o_(1))). • The estimate also has "back-up" worst-case error guarantee, i.e., even if the sub-paths lengths vary greatly, we incur an additive error of at most _O_(1) times the length of the path. 11We introduced part of our ideas for ED exclusively, but for additive _o(n_)-approximation, these two problems are equivalent since LCS is (mostly) a complementary version of ED.

For LCS, a minimization problem, we can simply let our back-up estimate be 0 when the sub-paths differ a lot in lengths, since this is always sound. For ED, we can use an off-the-shelf constant-factor approximation (e.g., \[CDG<sup>+</sup>20, GRS20, AN20\]) to obtain a sound back-up estimate with a multiplicative error of _O_(1).

### Putting it all together

If we never misestimate by more than a multiplicative factor of \(\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon'}{|\widetilde{S}|}\right)\) for each interval (_l,r_\] on an active scale for some \(\varepsilon'=o(1)\), the total error over \(\widetilde{S}\) active layers is bounded by:

\(\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon'}{|\widetilde{S}|}\right)^{|\widetilde{S}|}\approx(1+\varepsilon'),\)

which gives us a (1+_o_(1))-approximation. In our final algorithms, for an interval (_l,r_\] on an active scale, we use a simple concentration inequality to show that, for any specific path _p_ and interval (_l,r_\], the probability of mestimating the answer by more than \(\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon'}{|\widetilde{S}|}\right)\) due to sub-sampling is roughly \(2^{-M\frac{(\varepsilon')^2}{|\widetilde{S}|^2}}\) . Suppose that

\(M\gg log^{\Omega(1)}(n)/(\varepsilon')^2.\)

Then the probability of a large misestimation is \(2^{-log^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\). Even when we largely misestimate, the estimate inside an interval (_l,r_\] should never exceed its width _r-l_. Thus intuitively, the total additive error is expected to be bounded by \(n/2^{-log^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\) (we will formally show this using an observation on a special type of layered graphs (Claim 6.13)), which suffices since we assume the answer is _n/_2log<sup>_O_(1)</sup>(_n_).

## 3 Preliminaries

### 3.1 Notations

For \(i\in\mathbb{N}\), let \[_i_\] denote the set {1,2_,...,i_}.

For \(r\in\mathbb{R}\), let \(sign(r):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
-1, & \text{if}r\le 0 \\
+1, & \text{if}r>0
\end{array}\right.\) be the sign of _r_.

For a sequence _A_=(_a<sub>i</sub>_) of length _n_, we write \(\sum A\) to denote its sum \(\sum_{i=1}^na_i\).

### 3.2 Concentration Bound

As an ingredient for our analysis, we will use Hoeffding’s Inequality \[Hoe63\]:

**Lemma 3.1.** _Let X_=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>N</sub>_) _be N independent random variables in_ \[-_c,c_\]_. Then, for all_ \(\delta>0\),

\(\mathbf{Pr}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^Nx_i-\mu\right|\ge\delta\right)\le 2exp\left(-\frac{\delta^2}{2Nc^2}\right),\)

_where_ \(\mu=\mathbf{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^Nx_i\right]\).

### 3.3 Black-Box Calls to Existing ED and LCS Algorithms

We will use an _O_(1)-approximate ED algorithm, e.g., the following tradeoff proved in \[GRS20\]<sup>12</sup>:

**Lemma 3.2.** _Given two strings X and Y with lengths that sum to n, there is a randomized algorithm that computes a 4-approximation of_ ED(_X,Y_) _in O(n_<sup>1.61</sup>) _time._

We also use Ukkonen’s algorithm \[Ukk85\] for exact ED when the ED is small<sup>13</sup>:

**Lemma 3.3.** _Given two strings X and Y with lengths that sum to n and an upper bound k, there is an algorithm running in O(nk_) _time that can:_

• _Decide whether_ \(\mathrm{ED}(X,Y)\le k\);<tbc>

• _If_ \(\mathrm{ED}(X,Y)\le k\)_, compute_ ED(_X,Y_) _exactly._

When the LCS is small, the following result has been known since the 70s \[Hir77\]:

**Lemma 3.4.** _Given two strings X and Y with lengths that sum to n and an upper bound k, there is an algorithm running in O(nk+n_log(_n_)) _time that can:_

• _Decide whether_ \(\mathrm{LCS}(X,Y)\le k\);<tbc>

• _If_ \(\mathrm{LCS}(X,Y)\le k\)_, compute_ LCS(_X,Y_) _exactly_<sup>14</sup>.

### 3.4 Rounding

To avoid fractional results after divisions, for \(\lambda=2^{\lfloor 0.99\mathrm{log}(n)\rfloor}=\Theta(n^{0.99})\), we ensure that the lengths of two input strings are multiples of \(\lambda\) by padding them with arbitrary characters. The error we introduce with this rounding is \(O(\lambda)\), which is within (1+_o_(1)) when the ED/LCS is \(\omega(\lambda)\). When the ED/LCS is \(O(\lambda)\), we can use Lemma 3.3 or Lemma 3.4 to compute the answer exactly in \(O(n\lambda)=O(n^{1.99})\) time. Thus we can assume that input strings both have a length that is a multiple of a power of 2 of order \(\Omega(n^{0.99})\).

## 4 Tree Total Deviation

In this section we will introduce the notion of tree total deviation, which will be an important tool in analyzing our main algorithm for Edit Distance and LCS. We first introduce it in its basic form (Section 4.1). We then study a scaled variant of it (Section 4.2).

<sup>12</sup>We note that the choice of using \[GRS20\] is arbitrary. Since neither the running time nor the exact approximation factor is the bottleneck for our analysis, any of the truly sub-quadratic _O_(1)-approximation algorithms, starting with \[CDG<sup>+</sup>20\] and including \[CDG<sup>+</sup>20, And20, BR20, KS20b, AN20, RSSS25\] would suffice for our purpose. <sup>13</sup>There are faster algorithms for this problem, e.g., \[LMS98\]. However the difference would not translate to a qualitative improvement for our purposes. It is interesting that Ukkonen’s algorithm \[Ukk85\] also works for the more general setting of shortest paths on grids with diagonal shortcuts. Thus the only part in our algorithm for Edit Distance that requires actual strings is the _O_(1)-approximation algorithm from Lemma 3.2. <sup>14</sup>The original result states that there is an algorithm running in _O(n_LCS(_X,Y_)+_n_log(_n_)) time, this can easily be applied to the decision problem here by simply testing if the algorithm terminates within _O(nk+n_log(_n_)) time.

## 4.1 Basic Form

Given a sequence of real numbers _A_=(_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,...,a<sub>n</sub>_) with _n=M<sup>S</sup>_ for \(M\in 2\mathbb{Z}^+\) and \(S\in\mathbb{Z}^+\), we consider its _S_-scale recursive partition with branching factor _M_. In other words, for each scale \(s\in[S]\), we consider the partition of _A_ to disjoint length-_M<sup>s</sup>_ subsequences _A_<sub>(_l,r_]</sub>=(_a_<sub>_l_+1</sub>_,...,a<sub>r</sub>_). We say that (_l,r_] is a _scale-s interval_. Every interval (_l,r_] that is involved in the recursive partitioning (i.e., is a scale-_s_ interval for some scale \(s\in[S]\)) is called a _recursion interval_.

For a scale-_s_ interval (_l,r_], let the _i_-th (\(0\le i\le M\)) _anchor_ be \(m_i:=l+i\cdot\frac{r-l}{M}\) . Let (_m_<sub>_i_-1</sub>_,m<sub>i</sub>_] denote its _i_-th _sub-interval_. We consider the sum of each of _A_<sub>(_l,r_]</sub>’s sub-intervals, and compute the total deviation of the sums, namely the sum of how far each sub-interval is from the mean of the sub-intervals:

\(\mathrm{TD}_M(A_{(l,r]}):=\sum_{i=1}^M\left|A_{\Sigma(m_{i-1},m_i]}-\frac{1}{M}A_{\Sigma(l,r]}\right|,\)

where \(A'_{\Sigma(l^\prime,r^\prime]}\) denotes the sum \(\sum_{l^\prime<i\le r^\prime} a'_i\), a shorthand we will use throughout the paper.

We are particularly interested in the (_M_-way) _tree total deviation_, which sums the total deviation across the entire recursive partitioning of _A_:

\(\includegraphics{}\mathrm{TD}_{M,\mathcal{S}}(A):=\sum_{s\in[S]}\sum_{(l,r]\in s}\mathrm{TD}_M(A_{(l,r]}),\)

where we slightly abuse notation and use _s_ to denote both the scale and the set of scale-_s_ intervals. We also define a refined version of tree total deviation on a subset \(\mathcal{S}\subset[S]\) of scales.

\(\includegraphics{}\mathrm{TD}_{M,\mathcal{S}}(A):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{(l,r]\in s}\mathrm{TD}_M(A_{(l,r]}).\)

Intuitively, TD_<sub>M</sub>(A_) is a measure of how "uneven" _A_ is after dividing it into _M_ parts -- namely if we divide _A_ into _M_ parts, how far they are from all having the same sum. \(\includegraphics{}\mathrm{TD}_{M,\mathcal{S}}(A)\) is a measure of the sum of the total deviation of _A_ over all scales in S.

Suppose \(|a_i|\le 1\) for all _i_. A naive upper bound on TD<sub>_M,S_</sub>(_A_) would count a contribution of _O_(1) from each _a<sub>i</sub>_ to the total deviation on each scale, or TD<sub>_M,S_</sub>(_A_)=_O(nS_) in total. A key observation for our analysis is that in fact we can show that TD<sub>_M,S_</sub>(_A_) is close to \(n\sqrt{S}\):

**Lemma 4.1.** _Let A_=(_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,...,a<sub>n</sub>_) _be a sequence of real numbers where n=M<sup>S</sup>. Then,_

\(\includegraphics{}\mathrm{TD}_{M,S}(A)=O\left(\left(\sum_x|a_x|\right)S^{0.51}+\mathrm{max}_x|a_x|\cdot\left(n/2^{\mathrm{log}_M^{0.015}(n)}\right)\right).\)

**Definition 5.1** (Edit Distance Grid Graph)**.** The Edit Distance Grid Graph is a grid graph with diagonal shortcuts that can be used to compute ED(_X,Y_), and is defined as follows:

**Vertices** The grid points of \([0,n_X]\times[0,n_Y]\). The vertex at the intersection of the _x_-th column and the _y_-th row is \(\langle\langle x,y\rangle\rangle\);

**Edges** The set of edges includes standard grid edges and diagonal shortcut edges:

• Standard grid edges from \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle u,v+1\rangle\rangle\) or \(\langle\langle u+1,v\rangle\rangle\), always with weight 1 (corresponding to insertion or deletion);<tbc>

• Diagonal shortcut edges from \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) to \(\langle\langle u+1,v+1\rangle\rangle\), whose weight is 0 if _X_\[_u_\]=_Y_\[_v_\] (match) and 1 otherwise (substitution).

**Objective** ED(_X,Y_) is the length (sum of weights) of the shortest (0,0)-(_n<sub>X</sub>,n<sub>Y</sub>_) path.

Given two strings _X,Y_ of length _n<sub>X</sub>_ and _n<sub>Y</sub>_, we define an edge-weighted graph, corresponding to the profit of moving between states in the standard quadratic-time DP algorithm for LCS:

**Definition 5.2** (LCS Grid Graph)**.** The LCS Grid Graph is a grid graph with diagonal shortcuts that can be used to compute LCS(_X,Y_), and is defined as follows:

**Vertices** The grid points of \([0,n_X]\times[0,n_Y]\). The vertex at the intersection of the _x_-th column and the _y_-th row is \(\langle\langle x,y\rangle\rangle\);

**Edges** The set of edges includes standard grid edges and diagonal shortcut edges:

**Objective** LCS(_X,Y_) is the length (sum of weights) of the longest (0,0)-(_n<sub>X</sub>,n<sub>Y</sub>_) path.

## 5.1.2 Rotated Grid Graph: \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\rightarrow\langle u+v,v-u+n_X\rangle\)

To describe our algorithm, we will rotate the grids by 45 degrees and obtain graphs where for any fixed path, each column (corresponding to a diagonal in the original grid) is visited exactly once.

**Definition 5.3** (Rotated Edit Distance Grid Graph)**.** We use \(\langle\langle x,y\rangle\rangle\) to denote a vertex in the (original) Edit Distance Grid Graph at the intersection of column _x_ and row _y_ and \(\langle x,y\rangle\) to denote a vertex in the Rotated Edit Distance Grid Graph at the intersection of column _x_ and row _y_. The description of the new graph on the rotated grid is as follows:

**Vertices** The vertex for \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) in the original grid corresponds to \(\langle u+v,v-u+n_X\rangle\) on the new grid;

**Edges** We start with the same set of edges as in the original graph. Then, we divide each shortcut edge with weight \(w(\in\{0,1\})\) from \(\langle u,v\rangle\) to \(\langle u+2,v\rangle\) into two edges, one from \(\langle u,v\rangle\) to \(\langle u+1,v\rangle\) with weight 0 and the other from \(\langle u+1,v\rangle\) to \(\langle u+2,v\rangle\) with weight _w_.

**Objective** The length of the shortest \(\langle 0,n_X\rangle\)-\(\langle n_X+n_Y,n_Y\rangle\) path equals ED(_X,Y_).

**Definition 5.4** (Rotated LCS Grid Graph)**.** We use \(\langle\langle x,y\rangle\rangle\) to denote a vertex in the (original) LCS Grid Graph at the intersection of column _x_ and row _y_ and \(\langle x,y\rangle\) to denote a vertex in the Rotated LCS Grid Graph at the intersection of column _x_ and row _y_. The description of the new graph on the rotated grid is as follows:

**Vertices** The vertex for \(\langle\langle u,v\rangle\rangle\) in the original grid corresponds to \(\langle u+v,v-u+n_X\rangle\) on the new grid;

**Edges** We start with the same set of edges as in the original graph. Then, we divide each shortcut edge with weight \(w\left(\in\{0,1\}\right)\) from \(\langle u,v\rangle\) to \(\langle u+2,v\rangle\) into two edges, one from \(\langle u,v\rangle\) to \(\langle u+1,v\rangle\) with weight 0 and the other from \(\langle u+1,v\rangle\) to \(\langle u+2,v\rangle\) with weight _w_.

**Objective** The length of the longest path from \(\langle 0,n_X\rangle\) to \(\langle n_X+n_Y,n_Y\rangle\) equals LCS(_X,Y_).

For the remainder of the paper, a _path_ refers to a route from any \(\langle l,y_l\rangle\) to any \(\langle r,y_r\rangle\). Due to the split edges, any path _p_ in the grid graph from any column _l_ to any column _r_ visits each column \(x\in[l,r]\) exactly once. We denote by _p(x_) the y-coordinate (row) of the vertex \(\langle x,p(x)\rangle\) where the path crosses column _x_. By the construction of the rotated grid graphs, \(|p(x)-p(x-1)|\le 1\) for every \(l<x\le r\). For an interval \((l',r']\subset(l,r]\), we write \(p(l',r']\) to denote the sub-path of _p_ from \(l'\) to \(r'\). We define _w(p_) as the length (total weight of edges) of _p_.

We have the following observation:

**Observation 5.5.** For a path _p_, and for any two columns \(i\le j\) that the path visits,

\(|p(i)-p(j)|\le j-i.\)

_Proof._ We prove this by induction by increasing value of _j-i_. When _i=j_, the claim is trivially true since the path visits each column exactly once. Now suppose that the claim holds for _i,j_-1. The only edges from \(\langle j-1,p(j-1)\rangle\) go to \(\langle j,p(j-1)\rangle\), and (possibly) \(\langle j,p(j-1)\pm 1\rangle\). Therefore,

\(|p(i)-p(j)|\le|p(i)-p(j-1)|+1\le(j-1-i)+1=j-i.\)

Due to Observation 5.5, given two vertices \(\langle l,y_l\rangle\) and \(\langle r,y_r\rangle\), if \(\langle r,y_r\rangle\) is reachable from \(\langle l,y_l\rangle\), we must have \(|y_l-y_r|\le r-l\).

Plugging into (18), we have<tbc>

\(\sum_{k\in[S]}Y_k=O(\left|\widetilde{S}\right|w(p_{s^\prime})S^{0.51}/S^{0.98}).\)

## 6.2 Algorithm Description

Let \(\widetilde{S}\subset[S]\) be such that each scale is chosen u.a.r. with probability 1_/S_<sup>0.98</sup>. Our goal now is to approximate the length of the shortest \(\widetilde{S}\)-regular \(\langle 0,n_X\rangle\)-\(\langle n_X+n_Y,n_Y\rangle\) path \(\widehat{p}\):

**Lemma 6.6** (Restated)**.** _Let_ \(\widetilde{S}\subset[S]\) _be such that each scale is chosen u.a.r. with probability_ 1_/S_<sup>0.98</sup>_. Let_ \(\widehat{p}\) _be the shortest_ \(\widetilde{S}\)_-regular_ \(\langle 0,n_X\rangle\)_-_\(\langle n_X+n_Y,n_Y\rangle\) _path. With probability at least_ 3/4_, we can_ \((1\pm o(1))\)_- approximate_ \(w(\widehat{p})\) _in o(n_<sup>0.09</sup>) _time by querying only_ \(\frac{n^2\phi_y^2}{\mathcal{B}_x^2}/2^{\Omega\big(\mathrm{log}^{0.01}(n)\big)}\) _edge weights._

We can design an _M_-way _S_-scale divide-and-conquer scheme to compute \(\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[l,y_l,r,y_r]\) which is the length of the shortest \(\widetilde{S}\)-regular \(\langle l,y_l\rangle\)-\(\langle r,y_r\rangle\) path where (_l,r_\] is a scale-_s_ interval.

• If _s_=0, we obtain \(\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[l,y_l,r,y_r]\) using an edge weight query;<tbc>

• Suppose that _s\>_0 and \(s\notin\widetilde{S}\). Recall that the _i_-th anchor is \(m_i:=l+i\cdot\frac{r-l}{M}\) . We find \(\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[l,y_l,r,y_r]\) by minimizing over every anchor path defined by the sequence \(\widehat{Y}=(y_l=\widehat{y}_0,\widehat{y}_1,\dots,\widehat{y}_M=y_r)\), where for \(1\le i\le M\), \(|\widehat{y}_i-\widehat{y}_{i-1}|\le\frac{r-l}{M}\) , visiting valid vertices \((\langle m_i,\widehat{y}_i\rangle)_i\) in the sparsified grid graph. We use \(\unknown\) to denote the set of possible anchor paths \(\widehat{Y}\).<tbc>

• Suppose \(s\in\widetilde{S}\). Recall that we regularize the row after column _m<sub>i</sub>_ to \(\overline{y_i}:=(I_{s-1}/\phi_y)\cdot\left\lfloor\frac{y_l+i\frac{y_r-y_l}{M}}{I_{s-1}/\phi_y}\right\rfloor\). \(\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[l,y_l,r,y_r]\) is simply the sum of \(\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[m_{i-1},\overline{y_i},m_i,\overline{y_i}]\) over \(1\le i\le M\).

The full recursion is as follows:

\(\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{ew}[l,y_l,r,y_r], & \text{if}s=0 \\
\mathrm{min}_{\widehat{Y}\in\unknown}\sum_{i=1}^M\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[m_{i-1},\widehat{y}_{i-1},m_i,\widehat{y}_i], & \text{if}s\notin\widetilde{S} \\
\sum_{i=1}^M\widehat{\mathrm{ans}}[m_{i-1},\overline{y_i},m_i,\overline{y_i}], & \text{if}s\in\widetilde{S}
\end{array}\right..\) (20)

Unfortunately, this scheme still queries too many edge weights.

The key to efficiency is to use a _sub-sampling_ technique for active scales. We first show a naive attempt that can guarantee a small additive error (we later improve it to also obtain a bound on the multiplicative error). Notice that if \(s\in\widetilde{S}\), since no overfitting can happen when the path is fixed, we can just sample half of these values and double our sum from the sample. Thus, for every scale-_s_ interval (_l,r_\], we first uniformly randomly sample _M_ 0-1 variables \(\eta_{l,r,1\dots M}\) containing exactly _M/_21’s. We use the following scheme:

\(\mathrm{est}^*[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{ew}[l,y_l,r,y_r], & \text{if}s=0 \\
\mathrm{min}_{\widehat{Y}\in\unknown}\sum_{i=1}^M\mathrm{est}^*[m_{i-1},\widehat{y}_{i-1},m_i,\widehat{y}_i], & \text{if}s\notin\widetilde{S} \\
2\sum_{i=1}^M\eta_{l,r,i}\mathrm{est}^*[m_{i-1},\overline{y_i},m_i,\overline{y_i}], & \text{if}s\in\widetilde{S}
\end{array}\right.,\) (21)

Note that for every active scale, half of the sub-intervals (_m_<sub>_i_-1</sub>_,m<sub>i</sub>_\] for which \(\eta_{l,r,i}=0\) get discarded. Over \(\left|\widetilde{S}\right|\) active scales, only \(2^{-\left|\widetilde{S}\right|}\) fraction of the intervals remain, which is a significant speed-up.

Unfortunately, the scheme with (21) is not enough for a small multiplicative error, as \(\mathrm{est}^*[m_{i-1},\overline{y_{i-1}},m_i,\overline{y_i}]\) may be imbalanced over \(1\le i\le M\). In the most extreme example, if \(\mathrm{est}^*[m_{i-1},\overline{y_{i-1}},m_i,\overline{y_i}]\neq 0\) for only a single _outlier i_, then (21) either gets us an estimate that is 0 or an estimate that is twice the actual value, depending on the value of \(\eta_{l,r,i}\).

Due to the bound on tree total deviation, the weight distribution on the shortest path should intuitively not be imbalanced everywhere and there are not too many outliers in total. Thus even if we "give up" when we detect outliers, there should not be too much error. We first need to detect outliers. Recall that for each edge from \(\langle x,y\rangle\) to \(\langle x+\mathcal{B}_x,y'\rangle\), we are given a constant factor approximation \(\mathrm{aprew}[x,y,x+\mathcal{B}_x,y']\) of the edge weight \(\mathrm{ew}[x,y,x+\mathcal{B}_x,y']\). We can (detailed later) use this to obtain a constant-factor approximation \(\mathrm{appr}[l',y'_{l^\prime},r',y'_{r^\prime}]\) of the length of the shortest \(\langle l',y'_{l^\prime}\rangle\)-\(\langle r',y'_{r^\prime}\rangle\widetilde{S}\)-regular path for every valid \((l',y'_{l^\prime},r',y'_{r^\prime})\) where \((l',r']\) is a recursion interval. We now describe how we can obtain our estimate:

1. We detect outliers by checking if \(\mathrm{max}_{1\le i\le M}\mathrm{appr}[m_{i-1},\overline{y_{i-1}},m_i,\overline{y_i}]>\frac{\mathrm{appr}[l,y_l,r,y_r]}{M}\mathrm{loglog}(n)\).<tbc>

2. If \(\mathrm{max}_{1\le i\le M}\mathrm{appr}[m_{i-1},\overline{y_{i-1}},m_i,\overline{y_i}]\le\frac{\mathrm{appr}[l,y_l,r,y_r]}{M}\mathrm{loglog}(n)\), we let<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathrm{est}[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=\mathrm{min}\left(2\sum_{i=1}^M\eta_{l,r,i}\mathrm{est}[m_{i-1},\overline{y_i},m_i,\overline{y_i}],\mathrm{appr}[l,y_l,r,y_r]\right).\)<tbc>

<tbc>Namely we use the same formula as in (21), but clamp est\[_l,y<sub>l</sub>,r,y<sub>r</sub>_\] to at most appr\[_l,y<sub>l</sub>,r,y<sub>r</sub>_\] to make sure that est\[_l,y<sub>l</sub>,r,y<sub>r</sub>_\] does not over-estimate the answer worse than the constant-factor approximation does;<tbc>

3. If \(\mathrm{max}_{1\le i\le M}\mathrm{appr}[m_{i-1},\overline{y_{i-1}},m_i,\overline{y_i}]>\frac{\mathrm{appr}[l,y_l,r,y_r]}{M}\mathrm{loglog}(n)\), we simply "give up" and let est\[_l,y<sub>l</sub>,r,y<sub>r</sub>_\]:=appr\[_l,y<sub>l</sub>,r,y<sub>r</sub>_\], which still only gives us a multiplicative error of (1+_O_(1)).

<tbc>Given a path \(p'\) from column _l_ to column _r_, we let \(W(p')\) be the following sequence capturing the "weight distribution" of \(p'\):

\(W(p')=\left(w(p'(l,l+\mathcal{B}_x]),w(p'(l+\mathcal{B}_x,l+2\mathcal{B}_x]),\dots,w(p'(r-\mathcal{B}_x,r])\right)\)

\(\mathrm{est}[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }

\end{array}\right),\) (22)

<tbc>Unfortunately, this scheme still queries too many edge weights. The key to efficiency is to use a _sub- sampling_ technique for active scales. Notice that if \(s\in\widetilde{S}\), since no overfitting can happen when the path is fixed, we can just sample half of these values and double our sum from the sample. Thus, for every scale-_s_ interval (_l,r_\], we first uniformly randomly sample _M_0-1 variables \(\eta_{l,r,1\dots M}\) containing exactly _M/_21’s. We use the following scheme:

\(\text{est}^*[l,y_l,r,y_r]:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\text{ew}[l,y_l,r,y_r], & \text{if}s=0 \\

\end{array}\right..\) (31)

## A An Estimate-to-Search Reduction

In this appendix we give a reduction from the problem of searching an approximately optimal path on an ED/LCS grid with diagonal shortcuts (equivalently, ED transformation of insertions, deletions, and substitutions, or the actual longest common subsequence) to the problem of estimating the length of the optimal path (respectively, estimating the ED or the length of the LCS).

An \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-approximation of ED/LCS is an estimate within \([A,(1+\varepsilon)A+\delta]\) where _A_ is the true ED/LCS.

**Lemma A.1** (Estimate-to-Search)**.** _Given an algorithm_ A _that runs in time_ \(n^2/2^{\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\) _and estimates the ED/LCS between two input strings X,Y of lengths n<sub>X</sub>,n<sub>Y</sub>=O(n_) _to within_ \((\varepsilon(n),2^{\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)})\)_-approximation (i.e., the multiplicative approximation factor is a function on n), we obtain an algorithm_ \(\mathcal{A}'\) _that, runs in time_ \(n^2/2^{\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\) _and finds a transformation whose answer is an_ \((\varepsilon(\Theta(\sqrt{n})),2^{\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)})\)_-approximation of the optimal answer._

_Proof._ Let \(\gamma=2^{\mathrm{log}^c(n)}\) for some constant _c\>_0 be such that the running time of A is \(T(\mathcal{A},n)=O\left(n^2/2^{\mathrm{log}^{2c(n)}}\right)\). Let \(\mu=2^{\lfloor\mathrm{log}(n)/2\rfloor}=\Theta(\sqrt{n})\). We say a path _p_ on the Rotated Edit Distance/LCS Grid Graph is \(\gamma\)-rounded if for every \(\mu|x\), we have \(\lfloor\mu/\gamma\rfloor|p(x)\).

We can round the optimal path _p_ to a \(\gamma\)-rounded path using Lemma 5.9, incurring an additive error of only \(O(\sqrt{n}\cdot(\sqrt{n}/\gamma))=O(n/\gamma)=n/2^{\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)}\). Thus it suffices to find the optimal \(\gamma\)-rounded path.

Using A, we can approximate the length of the optimal \(\langle x,y\rangle\)-\(\langle x+\mu,y'\rangle\) path for every \(\mu|x\), \(\lfloor\mu/\gamma\rfloor|y,y'\) with \(|y-y'|\le\mu\). Since for each path we only need a \(\Theta(\mu)\cdot\Theta(\mu)\) sub-grid, the total running time is

\(O\left(\underbrace{\sqrt{n}\cdot 2^{\mathrm{log}^c(n)}\sqrt{n}}_\text{total number of sub-grids}\cdot\underbrace{\left(\sqrt{n}\right)^2/2^{\mathrm{log}^{2c}(\sqrt{n})}}_\text{time for each sub-grid}\right)=n^2/2^{\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)}.\)

We can use standard dynamic programming on a \(\gamma\)-rounded path \(\widehat{p}\) that is optimal with respect to the estimates computed by A. This gives us an \((\varepsilon(\Theta(\sqrt{n})),2^{\mathrm{log}^{\Omega(1)}(n)})\)-approximation of the optimal answer. This gives us \(\widehat{p}(x)\) for every column \(\mu|x\).

Finally we can fully recover \(\widehat{p}\) by using an exact algorithm for each of the sub-grids that contain a sub-path of \(\widehat{p}\). The exact algorithm runs in time quadratic in the side-length of the underlying sub-grids. Hence the total time of this part is

\(O\left(\underbrace{\sqrt{n}}_\text{number of sub-paths}\cdot\underbrace{\sqrt{n}\cdot\sqrt{n}}_\text{time for each sub-path}\right)=O(n^{1.5}).\)

<tbc>It remains to bound \(D(P\|U)\). We maximize \(\sum p_x\mathrm{ln}(np_x)\) subject to \(0\le p_x\le\|A\|_\infty/\|A\|_1\) and \(\sum p_x=1\). The divergence is maximized when the distribution is most concentrated (minimum entropy). Since \(p_x\le\|A\|_\infty/\|A\|_1\) for all _x_, we have:

\(D(P\|U)=\sum_xp_x\mathrm{ln}(np_x)\le\sum_xp_x\mathrm{ln}\left(n\frac{\|A\|_\infty}{\|A\|_1}\right)=\mathrm{ln}\left(\frac{n\|A\|_\infty}{\|A\|_1}\right).\)

Plugging this back into the tree deviation bound yields the lemma.

## C A Counter-Example to a Ratio-Free Version of Lemma 4.3

We provide an example showing that the \(\alpha\)-dependence of Lemma 4.3 is necessary, even for _M_=2: The authors are grateful to an anonymous reviewer for this construction.

**Lemma C.1.** _We can construct two sequences A_=(_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,...,a<sub>n</sub>_) _and B_=(_b_<sub>1</sub>_,b_<sub>2</sub>_,...,b<sub>n</sub>_) _of non- negative real numbers where n_=2_<sup>S</sup>, such that_

\(\includegraphics{}\text{SD}_{2,S}(A,B)=\Omega\left(S\sum_xb_x\right).\) (36)

_Proof._ We let _B_={1,1_,...,_1} simply be the length-_n_ sequence of 1’s. We let _A_={1,2,2,4,2,4,4,8_,..._} be the sequence where<tbc>

\(a_i=2^\text{number of 1’s in the binary representation of}(i-1).\)

<tbc>Notice that for every recursion interval (_l,r_\], we have \(\frac{A_{\Sigma(l,(l+r)/2]}}{A_{\Sigma((l+r)/2,r]}}=\frac{1}{2}\). Therefore \(\frac{\text{TD}_2(A(l,r])}{A_{\Sigma(l,r]}}=1/3\). Since \(B_{\Sigma(l,r]}=r-l\), we have \(\text{SD}_2(A(l,r],B(l,r])=\frac{r-l}{3}\) . Thus
